newsitem.title: UK: LME alloy contract will not die - Harris.
newsitem.headline: LME alloy contract will not die - Harris.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange aluminium alloy contract, which was launched in 1992 but has not traded very actively, is gaining moreacceptance and will continue, Chris Harris, director of marketing at Barclays Metals said.
"It has huge potential, as the (underlying) market for alloy will be six million tonnes in a few years' time...It will not die," Harris said at an LME metals seminar.
Like all new metals contracts launched on the LME, alloy has met with sceptimism from the industry. But others such as primary aluminium have overcome this.
Some of the problems with alloy, like storage, are being addressed, while the industry is also becoming more used to hedging procedures.
"A lot more scrap is now being priced on the LME, as scrap merchants are keen traders, Harris said.
This will increase, particularly in the case of new scrap, where intake is priced on a primary aluminium basis, but the scrap needs to be hedge sold against alloy.
Meanwhile, for the alloy industry as a whole, the LME contract will eventually lead to a much more uniform series of physical grades, he added.
